A gate of two bent hazel wands pegged into the stream bed, a fat rose-hip hung at the crown on a grass line, drooping low enough that every mast must duck, the left peg already tilting in the silt.

The turn marker: a rowanberry the colour of fire tethered to a sunken flint by a braid of reed-grass, bobbing hard in the current, a dragonfly riding it steadily in the opposite direction the race runs.

A start arch of two bulrush stems leaning from opposite banks, their tips lashed at the peak with sedge cord, a single dewdrop hung at the crossing on a milkweed-floss strand, swelling fat and ready to be struck.

The run's end: a garland of linked clover heads strung between two listing reeds above the surface, sagging to touch the water at its middle, four clover heads already chewed to bare stalks by something working from the left.

A count-twig of peeled birch laid across a mossy stone, nine river pebbles arranged along it, three knocked to the far end already, one sitting an inch below in the shallows where it rolled and nobody has fetched it back.

A gate of arched bramble shoot pegged into the gravel, a hawthorn berry hung dead centre on a grass thread, the berry so low a tall acorn-cap mast cannot pass without tilting, and a pale mayfly perched on the berry itself.

A second gate deeper on the course, its two reed-wand posts lashed with pine-resin to anchor stones, the crosspiece a length of plaited grass gone crooked mid-span where the resin dripped too thin and the cord slipped.

A mid-course gate of bent willow-withe, both peg ends tied to submerged pebbles, a loop of grass at the crown with one small elderberry dangling, spinning slowly in the eddy, the elderberry staining the current a faint wine-purple beneath.

A turn-post of a single cattail stem pushed into soft mud, a ring of woven rush near its base to hold it from tilting, the ring having tilted anyway, and a pond-snail climbing the stem in the wrong direction.

A signal drum of a large acorn cap lashed mouth-upward to a hazel stake at the bank, a beater of moss-wrapped grass beside it, and a scatter of last year's petals blown into the drumhead and softening the skin.

The second turn: a rose-hip on a braided sedge line pegged to a flat stone, a second smaller hip tied below the first for ballast, both hips spinning together in the current like a tiny double lantern.

A gate whose arch is a fresh bracken stem, still curling green at its tip, bent in a wide loop and both ends pressed into the bed with split-twig pegs, a single cranberry bead hung at its crown by a grass fibre.

The finish: a strand of dandelion-down stretched between two upright reed stems, both stems leaning inward from the pressure of the strand, so the whole gate tilts like a doorway in a storm and the down shimmers in the current's breath.

A checkpoint of two crossed twig wands lashed with rush cord forming an X above the water, a dried violet hanging at their crossing, its purple still vivid, stem looped through the lashing and one petal already detached, drifting downstream.

A half-gate for the shallows: one hazel wand bent from the bank and pegged into the opposite side with its tip only, a loop of grass trailing from the bend holding a rowanberry, the whole arm bowing lower as the flow pushes.

A pebble-count station: a flat stone the size of three boats, a peeled reed laid across its face, eleven small pale river pebbles along its length, and a slender fae in woven-grass clothes kneeling to move the fifth pebble with both hands.

A warning-post before the sharp bend: a tall bulrush pushed into the mud bank at a lean, a braid of bent grass wound around its midsection and tied off with a knot the size of an acorn, a dew-bead caught in the knot.

A gate of two green ash-keys bent into an arch, their own natural curl doing half the shaping, a red campion petal draped over the crown as a hanging marker, the petal folded once and held by a single thread of reed-fibre.

A finish-alternative garland of apple-blossom heads linked by their own stems, strung between two leaning reeds barely a thumb above the water, a bumblebee's weight already bending the third bloom down to kiss the surface intermittently.

A gust-chime of five empty hazelnut shells threaded on a single length of rush cord and hung from a low alder branch over the water, rattling together in the slightest draught to call the start fae to readiness on the bank.

The halfway point of the course shown by one fat rose-hip wedged between two forked twigs pushed into the bed and bound with pine resin, the hip glossy red and half under water, one twig already bowing downstream in the current.

A second signal post with an acorn-cap drum lashed above water-height to a willow stake, its beater a knob of soft moss on a hazel splint, the whole stake canted five degrees off true where the bank gave after last rain.

A gate repaired in the night: two reed posts with a crosspiece of bent grass cord, a visible binding of doubled rush at the mend, and a fresh rowanberry re-hung there to replace one that vanished, its grass tether still showing a pale raw knot.

The inner turn of the loop: a walnut shell weighted with a chip of flint, tethered on a plaited sedge line to a submerged root, rocking in the eddy, a water-boatman sitting perfectly still on its rim as though it owns the course.

A counting stone beside the bank: a broad flat grey pebble standing upright in the mud, eleven smaller white pebbles laid in a row along its top edge, one teetering at the far end, held from falling by a sprig of dried thyme.
